paragraphs: The main theme of the day is "meeting-arranging-monitoring-rescuing": in the morning, stand-up meetings are held to review progress, discuss risks with development, and review requirements with business; in the afternoon, they prioritize, handle changes, urge testing, and monitor joint debugging; in the evening, they write weekly reports and review risk lists. The launch period is the most stressful, as all links are in reverse order. If any link fails, a remedy must be devised immediately.

paragraphs: 7/10 explains that the "process layer" of IT project management is being heavily reconstructed by AI: documents, scheduling, minutes, and reports can all be automated, and the space for purely tool-based PM is shrinking. However, the success or failure of the project ultimately depends on decision-making and leadership. AI devalues ​​“managing things” and increases the value of “managing people and judgment”.

Medium and high exposure is a signal of evolution: stop being a "human Jira" - hand over the scheduling minutes to AI and spend your time on business understanding and team leadership. Project managers who understand both technology and business and can use AI to improve efficiency are scarce resources in the AI ​​era.

It is recommended to learn technology or business first, and then switch to project management - PMs without technical background are easily led away by the team. Computer and information management majors are related to each other. During college, I participated in many project practices. PM is something that can be "made" rather than "passed by exams".

Use AI project management tools to get rid of the role of document slave. Deepen business understanding and industry knowledge, obtain PMP or Agile certification, and at the same time maintain technical sensitivity and avoid being too far away from the front line.

There are advantages in transferring to PM in development, testing, product, and business positions. The key is to come up with "completely delivered project cases." During the interview, clearly explaining "what you have managed, how to schedule, and how to put out fires" is more useful than a bunch of certifications.

When recruiting PMs, don’t just look at certificates. Focus on business understanding, risk decision-making and upward management capabilities. Equip project managers with AI tools to reduce documentation burden, and focus assessments on delivery quality and team health.
